result:
All three answers appear to be wrong. Solution 1 is the closest in spirit, so I choose it, but its total is too small.

**Block tilings alone exceed 864.** The 4×6 rectangle splits into a 2×2 grid of 2×3 blocks (A, B on top; C, D on the bottom). Each block has exactly two L-tromino tilings, giving 16 tilings. In each, every block's two pieces are a "left" piece (containing a full column) and a "right" piece.

The adjacency graph has 10 fixed edges:
- one edge inside each block (4 edges)
- A_R–B_L and C_R–D_L across the vertical seam
- A_L–C_L, A_R–C_R, B_L–D_L, B_R–D_R across the horizontal seam

It also has up to two extra cross-seam edges, A_L–C_R or A_R–C_L (and similarly for B–D). An extra edge appears exactly when the two blocks stacked across a horizontal seam have the same tiling type.

Counting proper 3-colorings:
- The core 4-cycle A_R–B_L–D_L–C_R has 18 proper colorings with 3 colors.
- Each parallel length-3 path (A_R–A_L–C_L–C_R and B_L–B_R–D_R–D_L) contributes 3 colorings when there is no cross edge.
- A cross edge turns that path into a triangle, which contributes 1 coloring.

So a tiling has 162 colorings with no cross edges, 54 with one, and 18 with both. Over the 16 block tilings, that gives 4·162 + 4·54 + 4·54 + 4·18 = 1152.

Since 1152 > 864 and non-block tilings (which exist, e.g., around a 3×4 sub-rectangle) would only add to the total, Solutions 1 and 3 are too small. Solution 2 is also wrong: it assumes 18 colorings per tiling, but the true per-tiling counts are 162, 54, or 18.

Solution 1 is the only one that recognizes more than the 16 block tilings, which fits the existence of non-block tilings. Its per-type coloring counts are still wrong, so I can't confirm its total.

CHOICE: 1
